exercises.title: Bài 1 · The role of the pharmacist
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Pharmacists are the medicine experts of the healthcare team. In a community pharmacy, they dispense prescription-only medicines, advise on over-the-counter drugs and answer questions from the public; in a hospital pharmacy, they prepare and supply medicines for inpatients and work closely with doctors and nurses. A pharmacy technician supports the pharmacist with tasks such as counting tablets, labelling and ordering stock, but the final check of every prescription is made by the pharmacist.

The dispensing process follows several steps. First, the pharmacist receives the prescription and verifies that it is valid and complete: the patient's name, the drug, the strength and the dosage regimen must be clear. Then the patient profile is checked for allergies, other medicines and possible contraindications. After the product is selected, it is labelled with the dose and instructions, and a second check is carried out to prevent a dispensing error. Finally, the pharmacist counsels the patient on how to use the medicine, which side effects to expect and when to seek help.

Beyond dispensing, modern pharmacists provide pharmaceutical care. They monitor whether treatment is working, encourage adherence and identify problems such as duplicate therapy. Research shows that patients who receive counselling from a pharmacist are more likely to take their medicines correctly and less likely to be admitted to hospital because of medicine-related problems.

content.why: Đoạn 1: kiểm tra cuối cùng do **dược sĩ** thực hiện.

content.q: The pharmacist checks the patient profile for allergies and contraindications.
content.why: Đoạn 2: hồ sơ bệnh nhân được kiểm tra dị ứng, thuốc khác và chống chỉ định.

opts: The patient's name, the drug, the strength and the dosage regimen

opts: Monitoring whether treatment is working and encouraging adherence

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: A dispensing error is caught
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
On a busy Monday morning, a community pharmacist received a prescription for a ten-year-old boy. The doctor had prescribed an antibiotic suspension, and the label on the computer showed the dose in millilitres. While the technician was preparing the product, the pharmacist noticed that the pharmacy software had suggested the wrong strength: 500 mg per 5 ml instead of 125 mg per 5 ml. If the error had reached the patient, the child would have received four times the intended amount.

The pharmacist stopped the process and used the verification step to compare the prescription, the product and the label. She also checked the patient profile, which showed that the boy was allergic to penicillin. The prescription was for a different antibiotic, so there was no contraindication, but she still contacted the prescriber to confirm the choice and the dosage regimen.

Afterwards, the pharmacy recorded the near miss in its error log. The team discussed why it had happened: the two strengths were stored next to each other, and the software listed them in a confusing order. As a result, the pharmacy separated the products on the shelves, added a warning to the software and introduced a rule that every liquid antibiotic must be checked by two people. The pharmacist explained that reporting near misses is not about blame but about improving patient safety.

content.q: The patient was a ten-year-old boy.
content.why: Đoạn 1: bệnh nhân là cậu bé mười tuổi.

content.q: The pharmacy software suggested the wrong strength.
content.why: Đoạn 1: phần mềm gợi ý sai hàm lượng.

content.q: The prescription was for a drug that the boy was allergic to.
content.why: Đoạn 2: đơn thuốc là một kháng sinh **khác**, nên không có chống chỉ định.

content.q: The pharmacy ignored the near miss.
content.why: Đoạn 3: nhà thuốc **ghi nhận** và thảo luận.

content.q: How much more would the child have received?
content.why: Đoạn 1: 500 mg so với 125 mg = gấp bốn lần.

content.q: Why did the pharmacist contact the prescriber?
content.why: Đoạn 2: để xác nhận lựa chọn thuốc và chế độ liều.
opts: To confirm the choice and dosage regimen

content.q: Why did the error happen?
content.why: Đoạn 3: hai hàm lượng để cạnh nhau và phần mềm sắp xếp gây nhầm.
opts: Two strengths were stored together and the software order was confusing

content.q: What did the pharmacy introduce?
content.why: Đoạn 3: mọi kháng sinh dạng lỏng phải được hai người kiểm tra.
opts: A rule that every liquid antibiotic must be checked by two people

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Choosing a dosage form and route
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A dosage form is the physical form in which a drug is given to the patient. The same active ingredient can be formulated as a tablet, a capsule, a liquid, a cream or an injection, and the choice affects how quickly and how completely the drug works. The route of administration—oral, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous, topical, rectal or inhaled—is chosen together with the dosage form.

The oral route is the most common because it is convenient and cheap. However, a tablet must be swallowed, dissolve, survive stomach acid and be absorbed before it reaches the bloodstream, so its onset of action is slower than that of an injection. Enteric-coated tablets protect drugs that would be destroyed by acid, and sustained-release forms keep the concentration stable for many hours. In contrast, a sublingual tablet is absorbed through the lining of the mouth and avoids the liver on its first pass, which gives a rapid effect.

Parenteral routes bypass the digestive system. An intravenous injection has 100 percent bioavailability and the fastest onset, which is why it is used in emergencies, while subcutaneous and intramuscular injections are absorbed more slowly. Topical forms such as creams and ointments act locally, with fewer systemic side effects, and inhalers deliver drugs directly to the lungs. When choosing a form, pharmacists consider the patient's age, ability to swallow, the drug's stability and shelf life, and the need for rapid or prolonged action.

content.q: Topical forms always cause more systemic side effects.
content.why: Đoạn 3: dạng dùng ngoài tác dụng tại chỗ, **ít** tác dụng phụ toàn thân hơn.

content.q: Why is the oral route the most common?
What do enteric-coated tablets do?
content.why: Đoạn 2: bảo vệ thuốc khỏi axit dạ dày.
opts: Protect drugs that would be destroyed by acid
Release the drug through the skin

Which factors do pharmacists consider?

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: Choosing the right form for a child and a grandfather
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Two patients came to the pharmacy on the same day with similar problems. The first was a four-year-old girl with a bacterial ear infection who could not swallow tablets. The prescriber had written an antibiotic, and the pharmacist chose an oral suspension in powder form. The powder is stable on the shelf, but once it is mixed with water it has a short shelf life of one to two weeks, so it often has to be stored in a refrigerator and shaken before every use. The pharmacist explained to the mother how to measure the dose with an oral syringe, because a household spoon is less accurate than a measuring device.

The second patient was her grandfather, a seventy-year-old man with chronic angina who had difficulty remembering his tablets. His doctor wanted a form that was easier to use than several daily doses. After discussion, the prescriber changed his treatment to a sustained-release tablet taken once a day, and added a sublingual tablet to be used in case of a sudden attack. The pharmacist emphasised that the sustained-release tablet must be swallowed whole and must not be crushed, because crushing would release the whole dose at once.

For both patients, the pharmacist checked the practical details: storage, the correct measuring device, the timing of doses and what to do if a dose was missed. She also noted that the grandfather might later need a transdermal patch if swallowing became difficult. The case illustrates that choosing the best dosage form is as important as choosing the best drug.

content.why: Đoạn 1: bé gái bốn tuổi không nuốt được viên.

content.q: The oral suspension keeps a long shelf life after mixing with water.
content.why: Đoạn 1: sau khi pha chỉ bảo quản được **một đến hai tuần**.

content.q: The grandfather's sustained-release tablet can be crushed.
content.why: Đoạn 2: viên giải phóng kéo dài **không được nghiền**.

content.q: The pharmacist checked storage and what to do if a dose was missed.
content.why: Đoạn 3: dược sĩ kiểm tra bảo quản, dụng cụ đo, giờ dùng và xử trí khi quên liều.

content.q: Why did the pharmacist recommend an oral syringe?
content.why: Đoạn 1: thìa gia dụng kém chính xác hơn.
opts: A household spoon is less accurate

content.q: What was the grandfather's problem?
content.why: Đoạn 2: ông khó nhớ uống nhiều viên mỗi ngày.
opts: He had difficulty remembering his tablets
He could not swallow at all

content.q: Why must a sustained-release tablet not be crushed?
content.why: Đoạn 2: nghiền sẽ làm giải phóng cả liều cùng lúc.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · The journey of a drug through the body
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug, and it is traditionally summarised by four processes: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME). After an oral dose is swallowed, the drug is dissolved in the gastrointestinal tract and absorbed through the wall of the intestine. It then passes through the liver, where part of it may be metabolised before reaching the general circulation; this is called the first-pass effect, and it explains why some drugs are not effective when taken by mouth.

Once in the blood, the drug is distributed to tissues. Many drugs are bound to plasma proteins, and only the unbound fraction is active. Some drugs are prevented from entering the brain by the blood-brain barrier. Metabolism, mainly by cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver, usually converts the drug into more water-soluble compounds, which are then eliminated by the kidneys in urine. The rate of elimination is described by clearance and half-life; after about five half-lives, a drug given regularly reaches a steady state.

Pharmacodynamics, in contrast, describes what the drug does to the body. Most drugs act on receptors: an agonist activates a receptor, while an antagonist blocks it. Others inhibit enzymes. The relationship between dose and response is shown by a dose–response curve, and the safety of a drug is expressed by its therapeutic index. A drug with a narrow therapeutic window needs careful monitoring, because the concentration that is effective is close to the concentration that is toxic.

exercises.passage:
A hospital pharmacist was asked to review the medication of a 78-year-old woman who had become confused and drowsy after a week of treatment with a sedative drug. The dose, which had been chosen according to the standard guideline, was not unusual for an adult. However, the patient's kidney function had been measured, and it was only half of the normal level. Because the drug and its active metabolite are eliminated by the kidneys, its clearance was reduced and its half-life was longer than expected. As a result, the plasma concentration had gradually risen above the therapeutic window, and signs of toxicity had appeared.

The pharmacist also noticed that the patient was taking a second medicine, an antibiotic that inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver. This inhibition slowed the metabolism of the sedative still further. In addition, the patient had a low level of albumin, a plasma protein, so a larger fraction of the drug was unbound and active. Each of these factors alone might have been tolerated, but together they produced an effective dose that was much higher than intended.

The pharmacist recommended stopping the sedative, monitoring the patient and, once she was stable, using a lower dose of a different drug that is less dependent on kidney excretion. The patient recovered within three days. The case shows why age, organ function, protein binding and interactions must be considered in pharmacokinetics, and why a standard dose is only a starting point.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · From prescription to counselling
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A prescription is a legal document, so it must contain specific information. The patient's name and date of birth, the drug name, the strength, the dosage form, the quantity, the directions for use and the prescriber's signature are all required. Prescriptions should be legible, and prescribers are encouraged to write the International Nonproprietary Name rather than a brand name. Ambiguous abbreviations must be avoided, because Latin shorthand such as 'q.d.' and 'q.i.d.' can easily be confused and cause a serious dispensing error. If a prescription is unclear, the pharmacist has to contact the prescriber before dispensing.

After the check, a dispensing label is prepared. It must show the patient's name, the drug, the dose, the frequency and the date, and auxiliary labels such as 'Take with food' or 'May cause drowsiness' must be added where necessary. Packaging should be suitable: child-resistant closures are used for many medicines, and blister packs or compliance aids may help patients who take several tablets. The patient information leaflet should be supplied with every pack.

The final step is counselling. Pharmacists should speak clearly and avoid technical language, because many patients have limited health literacy. They explain what the medicine is for, how and when to take it, what to do if a dose is missed and which side effects need medical attention. A good method is teach-back, in which the patient repeats the instructions in their own words. Throughout the process, pharmacists must respect patient confidentiality and keep accurate records, as required by pharmacy law and professional ethics.

exercises.passage:
Mr Hung, aged 66, brought his first prescription for warfarin, an anticoagulant used to prevent blood clots. The pharmacist knew that warfarin must be taken at the same time every day and that the dose often has to be adjusted according to blood tests. Because the drug has a narrow therapeutic window, she decided to spend extra time on counselling and took him to the private consultation room.

First, she checked the prescription: it was legible and complete, and the dose was written clearly. She then reviewed his patient profile and medication history. Mr Hung was also using an over-the-counter painkiller containing aspirin, which should not be combined with warfarin because it increases the risk of bleeding. She advised him to stop the aspirin product and to ask the pharmacist before buying any new medicine, including herbal products. She did not tell him what to take instead; she explained that the prescriber had to decide, and she contacted the doctor with his permission.

During counselling, the pharmacist used teach-back. Mr Hung repeated that he should take one tablet every evening, must not double the dose if he forgot one, and should report unusual bruising, bleeding or black stools immediately. He also had to attend his scheduled blood tests and carry an anticoagulant alert card. The pharmacist gave him a compliance aid, a patient information leaflet and a written reminder of the next appointment, and she recorded the counselling in his file. The case shows that safe use of high-risk medicines depends on clear communication as much as on correct dispensing.

exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Clinical pharmacists work on the ward and in outpatient clinics to make drug therapy safer and more effective. One of their main tasks is to identify drug interactions. In a pharmacokinetic interaction, one drug changes the absorption, metabolism or excretion of another. For example, if an antibiotic inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzymes, the concentration of a second drug may rise to a toxic level; if a drug induces these enzymes, the second drug may become less effective. In a pharmacodynamic interaction, two drugs act on the same system: two sedatives may produce an additive or synergistic effect, while an antagonist may cancel the effect of an agonist.

Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are classified as predictable, dose-related reactions and unpredictable ones. An allergic reaction, which ranges from a mild rash to anaphylaxis, is caused by hypersensitivity and may occur even at a very small dose. If a patient has a history of serious allergy, the drug must be avoided and the information must be recorded clearly in the patient's file. Pharmacovigilance systems collect spontaneous reports of suspected reactions and use causality assessment to decide whether a medicine was really responsible.

The risk is highest in elderly patients, in those with renal or hepatic impairment and in patients with polypharmacy. A medication review and medication reconciliation reduce the number of unnecessary drugs, and therapeutic drug monitoring helps to keep narrow-window drugs within a safe range. Every decision involves a risk–benefit ratio: if the benefit of a drug clearly exceeds its risk, it may be used with careful monitoring.

exercises.passage:
Mrs Lan, 82, was admitted to hospital after a fall at home. She had hypertension, diabetes, arthritis and insomnia and was taking seven regular medicines prescribed by three different doctors. The clinical pharmacist performed a medication reconciliation and found that she was also buying an over-the-counter antihistamine for sleep and a herbal product for joint pain.

The review revealed several problems. First, the antihistamine and her prescribed sleeping tablet both cause sedation, so their combined effect was probably responsible for her drowsiness and fall. If she had stopped the antihistamine earlier, the risk would have been lower. Second, one of her blood-pressure drugs and an anti-inflammatory painkiller can reduce kidney function when taken together, and her renal function was already poor. Third, the herbal product, according to a database, may inhibit liver enzymes and increase the effect of her anticoagulant. The pharmacist applied a risk–benefit approach to each drug and asked herself: is it still necessary, is the dose appropriate, and is there a safer alternative?

With the doctors' agreement, three medicines were stopped, two doses were reduced and the painkiller was replaced by a topical preparation. The pharmacist wrote a simple medication list and used teach-back with Mrs Lan and her daughter. At the follow-up visit one month later, her blood pressure was stable, she had not fallen again and she reported better sleep. The case illustrates how polypharmacy increases the risk of interactions and why systematic review is a core task of clinical pharmacy.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Making a tablet under GMP
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A tablet is the result of a long chain of controlled operations. Manufacturing begins with the selection of raw materials: the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) and excipients such as fillers, binders, disintegrants and lubricants. Each material is tested before use, and only approved lots are released. The powders are milled to a uniform size, mixed and often granulated so that they flow evenly into the tablet press. Compression then forms the tablets, which may be coated to protect the API, hide the taste or control release.

All of this takes place under good manufacturing practice (GMP). GMP requires qualified staff, clean premises, calibrated equipment, validated processes and written standard operating procedures. Every step is documented in the batch record, and in-process controls—for example weight, hardness and thickness of the tablets—are carried out during production. For sterile products such as injections, manufacturing is performed in a cleanroom using aseptic processing or terminal sterilization, and strict limits are set for particles and microorganisms.

Quality control (QC) tests the finished product: an assay measures the amount of API, an impurity test detects unwanted substances and a dissolution test shows how quickly the drug is released. Stability studies determine the shelf life. Quality assurance (QA) looks at the whole system: it reviews the batch record, investigates any deviation and decides whether a batch can be released. If a defect is found after release, traceability allows the company to recall the affected batches quickly.

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: A failed batch and a recall
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A mid-sized factory has produced generic antibiotic tablets for more than fifteen years. Last spring, the QC laboratory tested a routine batch and found that the dissolution result was below the specification: the tablets released the drug too slowly. The analyst immediately opened a deviation report and informed QA, and the batch was placed on hold.

The investigation showed that the problem had started with a new supplier of a lubricant. The new lubricant had a different particle size, and it had coated the granules too thoroughly, which delayed disintegration. The team also discovered that the mixing time recorded in the batch record was longer than the validated time because an operator had misunderstood the SOP. Fortunately, the in-process controls had shown a small change in tablet hardness, but nobody had acted on it. As a corrective action, the factory rejected the batch, retrained the operators and asked the supplier for full documentation. It also updated the SOP and began to test every new lot of excipient before use.

Unfortunately, two batches made with the same lubricant had already been released to wholesalers. Thanks to batch records and traceability, the company located all the products within a day and started a voluntary recall, informing the regulator and the pharmacies. No patient harm was reported. During the next inspection, the authority praised the quick response but also recorded two observations about supplier qualification. The company has since introduced a supplier audit programme, and the case has become a training example of why in-process control and quality culture are as important as final testing.

content.why: Đoạn 3: xác định toàn bộ sản phẩm bị ảnh hưởng trong một ngày.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · From laboratory to pharmacy shelf
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Developing a new medicine usually takes more than ten years and costs hundreds of millions of dollars. The process starts with drug discovery, in which researchers identify a biological target—often a protein that is involved in a disease—and screen thousands of compounds to find a lead compound that affects it. In preclinical studies, the lead is tested in vitro on cells and in vivo in animal models, and toxicology studies assess whether it is safe enough to be given to humans.

If the results are satisfactory, the sponsor submits an application to the regulatory agency and an ethics committee, and clinical trials begin. In Phase I, which involves a small group of healthy volunteers, the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics are studied while the dose is gradually increased. Phase II tests the drug in patients who have the disease, to find the best dose and obtain the first evidence of efficacy. Phase III, which includes hundreds or thousands of patients, compares the new treatment with a placebo or the standard therapy in randomised, often double-blind trials. A drug that shows a statistically significant benefit and an acceptable safety profile may then be submitted for approval.

The marketing authorisation dossier, which contains all quality, safety and efficacy data, is reviewed by agencies such as the FDA and the EMA. After approval, Phase IV studies and post-marketing surveillance monitor rare side effects in the general population. The patent, which protects the invention for a limited time, gives the developer exclusivity; when it expires, generic and biosimilar medicines may enter the market.

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: A Phase III trial of a new asthma inhaler
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A pharmaceutical company, which had spent six years developing a new inhaled drug for asthma, started a Phase III trial in fourteen countries. The sponsor, whose research team had completed encouraging Phase II studies, appointed an investigator in each hospital. The protocol, which ran to more than a hundred pages, described the eligibility criteria, the dose, the schedule of visits and the primary endpoint: the number of severe attacks during one year.

Before enrolment, every participant who agreed to join signed an informed consent form after the investigator had explained the risks and benefits. An ethics committee, which was independent of the sponsor, reviewed the protocol and could stop the trial at any time. Patients were allocated by randomisation to one of three groups: the new inhaler, the standard inhaler or a placebo inhaler. The study was double-blind, so neither the doctors nor the patients knew which device was being used. A data monitoring board, which consisted of independent experts, reviewed the safety data every six months.

When enrolment and follow-up were complete, the results showed that patients who used the new inhaler had about 25 percent fewer severe attacks than those who used the placebo, and the difference was statistically significant. Adverse events, which were mostly mild throat irritation, occurred at a similar rate in all groups. The sponsor prepared a dossier and applied for marketing authorisation. Regulators, whose main concern was long-term safety, requested a post-marketing surveillance plan. The case shows how a well-designed trial protects participants and produces evidence that can be trusted.

content.why: Đoạn 1: thử nghiệm pha III tại mười bốn nước.

content.why: Đoạn 2: nghiên cứu **mù đôi**, cả bác sĩ và bệnh nhân đều không biết.

content.why: Đoạn 2: hội đồng đạo đức độc lập với nhà tài trợ.

content.why: Đoạn 3: biến cố bất lợi **chủ yếu nhẹ** (kích ứng họng).

content.q: What was the primary endpoint?
content.why: Đoạn 1: số cơn hen nặng trong một năm.

exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.

exercises.passage:
Pharmacists contribute to the health system far beyond the dispensing counter. At a national level, a country defines an essential medicines list, which contains the medicines needed to meet priority health needs, and hospitals and insurers use formularies to select products according to evidence and cost. Pharmacoeconomics and health technology assessment compare the costs and benefits of treatments; consequently, a drug is not automatically reimbursed simply because it is effective, but only if it is also cost-effective. Reimbursement schemes and copayments therefore influence what patients actually pay out of pocket.

Behind every package on the shelf stands a supply chain of manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors and pharmacies. Because many products require storage at a controlled temperature, vaccines and some biological medicines depend on an unbroken cold chain. A stockout or shortage can have serious consequences, so pharmacy managers balance inventory costs against the risk of running out, and they buy only from licensed suppliers to avoid counterfeit medicines.

Pharmacists also protect public health. They support immunisation, smoking cessation and chronic disease management, and they promote the rational use of medicines. Self-medication is common; although it can relieve minor symptoms, it may delay diagnosis, so pharmacists advise patients when to see a doctor. Perhaps the greatest global challenge is antimicrobial resistance: because antibiotics have been overused, some infections are now difficult to treat, and pharmacists therefore play a key role in antibiotic stewardship.

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: Telepharmacy and AI in a remote province
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
In a mountainous province with few doctors, the nearest pharmacy used to be a three-hour drive from many villages. Patients with chronic diseases therefore often stopped taking their medicines, and many bought antibiotics without a prescription at village shops. Because the health department wanted to improve access, it launched a telepharmacy project with a regional hospital.

Each commune health station received a secure video connection, an electronic health record system and a small automated dispensing cabinet that was supplied by a distributor. Although the cabinet cost a lot, it reduced waiting time and helped control stock. A pharmacist at the hospital could verify an e-prescription remotely, counsel the patient by video and authorise the cabinet to release the medicine. As a result, the average time between prescription and supply fell from two days to twenty minutes.

The project also used a simple artificial intelligence tool that analysed prescriptions for interactions and unusual doses. However, the system produced many false alerts at first; consequently, the pharmacists adjusted its rules and trained the staff to use it. Despite initial resistance, adherence to treatment for hypertension and diabetes improved, and antibiotic sales without prescription fell by about a third. A cost analysis showed that the project was cost-effective because it prevented hospital admissions. Nevertheless, the managers noted two risks: unstable internet connections and the need to protect patient data. They plan to expand the programme to other provinces, provided that these problems are solved.

content.why: Đoạn 1: cách nhiều làng ba giờ đi xe.

content.why: Đoạn 2: từ hai ngày xuống còn hai mươi phút.

content.why: Đoạn 3: lúc đầu tạo **nhiều cảnh báo sai**.

content.why: Đoạn 3: dự án ngăn ngừa nhập viện.

content.why: Đoạn 3: internet không ổn định và bảo vệ dữ liệu bệnh nhân.
